Getting Started

This series of courses is a practical guide to coding for biologists. The empahasis is on developing the skills to work with genomic data.

The courses introduce the scripting language R, before covering the basics of biological Data and how to process it.

Each course can be used independently, but the logic and skills build from one to the other. So if you are new to this we advise you start at the beginning.

Course Order

  1. Intro To R
  2. Plotting In R
  3. Genomic Data
  4. IGV
  5. Introduction to Bioconductor
  6. ChIPseq
  7. ATACseq
  8. RNAseq
  9. Genomic Variants
  10. Vizualising genomics data in R and Bioconductor

Course make up

  • The course is presented as both presentations and single-pages (HTML) and the R code.
  • Exercises and answer sheets are included after all subsections to practice techniques and provide future reference examples.

Setting up

  • Before starting it is essential that you install R.
  • We also recommend installing RStudio.
  • This a integrated development environment, with an easy to use graphic interface that makes R much more palatable.

Install R.

  • R can be installed from the R-project website.
  • R 3.6.0 or higher is recomended for this course.

http://www.r-project.org/

Install RStudio.

  • RStudio can be installed from the R-project website.

http://www.rstudio.com/

Install required packages.

  • First launch RStudio
  • Install the packages in the R console using install.packages
install.packages("ggplot2",dependencies=TRUE)
install.packages("rmarkdown",dependencies=TRUE)
install.packages("yaml",dependencies=TRUE)

How to communicate with us

  • Sometimes you may need a hand with the training or you may notice a bug/mistake.

  • The best practise for reaching out to us is through GitHub, as this is where we host all our courses.

Why can’t I just email you?

You can. But we discourage this. A lot of people have the same question. By posting the issue on GitHub, it allows us to reply publically. This means future users with the same question will not have to wait for us to respond.

That said you can get our contact information here to reach out to us directly: https://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/

What is GitHub?

  • GitHub is an essential tool for anyone interested in programming. It allows easy sharing and collaboration whilst also promoting good coding practises through version control.

  • We will be addressing how to use GitHub fully soon with a workshop.

  • Here we will show specifically what you need to do to raise an issue.

Make a GitHub account

  • Go to the GitHub website
  • Sign up for an account (you can also apply for a pro account if you are affiliated with an educational institute)

Visit our repositories

  • All our courses can be found at The Rockefeller University GitHub
  • Each course is in its own repository (collections of code for a single project).
  • Several courses are pinned to the top. If the course you are working on isn’t pinned you can either scroll down to find the relevant repository or use the search bar.

imagename

Check open issues

  • Once in the repository click the Issue tab.
  • Any open issues will be displayed. Open means we are working on fixing them at the moment.
  • Click the closed issue. Check through the previous issues to see if any are relevant to your question.
  • If there are a lot of issues the search bar can be used. Searching forgiving like google, so you will need an exact match to something in the closed issue.

imagename

Create a new issue

  • If there are no previous relationships realted to your question/bug then create a new one by pressing the green “New Issue” button.
  • Give the Issue a title and describe the question/bug. Be as clear and concise as possible. If you can slide numbers or section titles that will help. You can also add images like screenshots with simple drag and drop.

imagename

Bug fixes

  • For those familiar with the GitHub ecosystem that run into an error we encourage users to make their own corrections.
  • This can be for errors as simple as Typos or larger problems such as bugs in the code itself
  • Once you have created the issue, just fork the repository, make edits, create a pull request and we will review your changes before merging them.
